objective: By the end of this lesson you can recognize the moment you become doubtful of your position, fix it with landmarks, VOR, GPS or ATC, judge how much fuel and daylight you really have, and choose when to ask for help, declare an emergency or land, the way a pilot carrying paying passengers is expected to.
why: The AIM says you are in at least an urgency condition the moment you become doubtful about your position or fuel, and that delay has cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Getting lost is most dangerous when fuel is low [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]], and 'being lost' is one of the FAA's listed reasons for a precautionary landing [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. A commercial pilot is expected to act early, not hope.

warmup: Think first: you are 40 minutes into a charter flight with two passengers. The town ahead does not match your chart and the GPS tablet just went dark. You have about 75 minutes of fuel and sunset is in 50 minutes. Which runs out first, and what is the very first thing you do with your hands and your eyes?

key_terms.def: Concern about safety that needs timely but not immediate help; a potential distress condition [[34:437|P/CG Urgency]]. Being doubtful about your position puts you in at least this condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].
Serious or imminent danger that needs immediate help [[34:337|P/CG Distress]]. The radio signal is MAYDAY [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
The last place you were sure of, with its time and the heading flown since. The AIM asks for it in the emergency call when you are lost [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
Navigation by computation from time, airspeed, distance and direction; it gives heading and groundspeed [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].
Long features on each side of the course, such as highways, rivers or railroads, that you do not cross, so you cannot drift far off course [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
The highest terrain or obstacle elevation within a sectional quadrant, rounded up to the next 100 ft, with the last two digits not shown [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p. 12]].
Headings from a radar controller to a VFR aircraft that can talk to the facility, is in radar coverage and is radar identified. They are advisory; flying safely stays your job [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].
A facility finds you by your radio signal: you hold the transmit button a few seconds, release, and may be asked to turn and repeat [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
A thin-line chart box; frequencies above it are remoted to that NAVAID site so you can reach a Flight Service Station from far away [[2:51|Chart Users' Guide p. 51]].
Minutes of flight left until fuel exhaustion, including reserve fuel and an allowance for fuel gauge error [[34:349|P/CG Fuel Remaining]].
You can accept little or no delay at your destination. It is not an emergency and does not give you priority [[34:379|P/CG Minimum Fuel]] [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].
A planned landing, on or off an airport, when further flight is possible but unwise; being lost and a fuel shortage are listed examples [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

chunks.title: Lost procedures at the commercial level

body.p: Getting lost is dangerous, most of all when fuel is low [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. The FAA does not wait for you to be completely lost: you are in at least an urgency condition the moment you become doubtful about your position, fuel endurance, weather or anything else that could hurt the flight. That is the time to ask for help, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

The commercial ACS Task has the same elements, word for word, as the private Task: methods to find position (K1), help available (K2), four risk items (R1 to R4) and five skills (S1 to S5) (ACS CA.VI.D; ACS PA.VI.D). Neither ACS gives a number tolerance for this Task. The difference is what the examiner expects from a pilot who may soon carry people for hire: faster recognition, a clear plan, and honest use of ATC.

head: Tool
What it gives you
Source
rows: Position from features you can name on the chart, like a town name on a water tower
An estimate from your last fix, heading, groundspeed and time
A fix where azimuths from two or more stations cross
Your position and the nearest airport
Radar vectors, DF steering, and search and rescue

body.p: The PIC is the final authority for the flight. In an in-flight emergency that needs immediate action, you may deviate from any rule of Part 91 as far as needed to meet it, and you must send a written report if the FAA asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

callout.text: Many instructors teach a 'Cs' list (climb, communicate, confess, comply, conserve, and sometimes circle). No FAA source used here prints that list. Treat it as a memory aid only; each part that is in the sources is cited where it is taught in this lesson.

check.q: At what moment does the AIM say a pilot is in at least an urgency condition?
check.a: The moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather or anything else that could adversely affect safety [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

chunks.title: Stay found: times, last fix and the flight plan

body.p: Dead reckoning works only from a known point. The predicted heading keeps you on the path and the groundspeed sets the time to each checkpoint; pilotage then checks and corrects both [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]. As the trip goes on, note headings and times and adjust heading, groundspeed and ETA [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

Why the time matters when you are lost: the AIM emergency message asks for your present position and heading, or, if lost, your last known position, the time there and the heading since [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Without a written time over your last checkpoint you cannot answer, and nobody can draw a search area.

bullets: Distance from your last fix = groundspeed x time since it. 18 minutes at 110 knots is 18 x 110 / 60 = 33 NM (application of [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]).
That distance is the radius of your 'where could I be' circle. The longer you wait, the bigger it gets.
Never rely on one checkpoint. If you miss one, keep the heading and look for the next one [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

body.p: The flight plan is the other half of staying found. A filed flight plan is the most timely sign that an aircraft is overdue [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. If you do not answer within half an hour after your ETA, a search starts. If your ETE changes by 30 minutes or more, give the nearest FSS a new ETA; if you land somewhere else, report it [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

callout.text: If you are on radar flight following and lose both radar and radio without a service termination, the facility treats it as a possible emergency and search and rescue may start [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. Tell ATC before you change frequency or leave.
Commercial habit: say your checkpoint, time and fuel out loud as you write them. If a passenger asks where you are, you should be able to answer from the log, not the screen.

check.q: You last confirmed your position at 1412 and it is now 1430. Groundspeed is about 110 knots. What is the most you could be from that fix?
check.a: 18 x 110 / 60 = 33 NM, using groundspeed and time from the last known point (dead reckoning, [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]).

chunks.title: The first minute: hold the heading and climb

body.p: When a checkpoint does not show up, the first move is to keep flying straight. The PHAK says: if confused, hold the heading; turning away from it is how pilots become lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. A steady heading keeps your dead reckoning useful, so your last fix still means something.

Then climb, if traffic and weather allow. Altitude increases radio and navigation reception range and radar coverage [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. The AIM gives the same advice for any distress or urgency: climb, if possible, for better communications and better radar and direction finding detection [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]]. Radar and ADS-B coverage are line of sight, and a low altitude can lose contact; climbing improves it [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]].

head: Limit on the climb
Why
Source
rows: Below 10,000 ft MSL in Class E: 3 SM, 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal from clouds
No unauthorized climb in IFR conditions in controlled airspace
Use the quadrant MEF; never get closer than 500 ft above the tallest antenna

body.p: The MEF is a quick floor for a climb when you are unsure of exactly where you are. It is the highest elevation in a quadrant of 30 minutes of latitude by 30 minutes of longitude, terrain and obstacles included, rounded up to the next 100 ft [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p. 12]]. For a natural feature, the FAA adds the possible vertical error and a 200 ft allowance for uncharted obstacles, then rounds up [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p. 13]]. Because you may be in the next quadrant, look at the MEFs around your estimated area too (application).

callout.text: The 'circle' in some memory aids is not in the FAA text used here. Circling destroys your heading and time record, the very things the PHAK tells you to keep [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. If you orbit, do it over a landmark you have positively identified, while you talk to ATC (CFI technique, not FAA text).

check.q: Give the two reasons the sources give for climbing when lost.
check.a: Better radio and navigation reception range and better radar coverage [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]; the AIM adds better direction finding detection [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]].

body.p: Good checkpoints are prominent features that can be confirmed by other features near them: roads, rivers, railroad tracks, lakes and power lines [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. When lost, work from big to small. Find a large feature you cannot mistake, then confirm with a second one nearby. Near a town, you may be able to read its name on a water tower [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

bullets: A small black square with a short description marks the exact spot of landmarks seen easily from the air, such as stadiums, pumping stations and refineries. A small black circle marks water, oil or gas tanks [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p. 10]].

Man-made obstacles are usually charted when they are more than 200 ft AGL. Features ATC uses as checkpoints have a black graphic symbol with the MSL top and AGL height in blue [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p. 11]].

In dense city areas only the highest obstacle may be shown, with a group obstacle symbol [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p. 11]]. In congested areas some smaller features are left off the chart [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
New roads and buildings may not be on the chart until the next edition, and antennas can be hard to see [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

body.p: Scale check: on a sectional, 1 inch is 8 SM or 6.86 NM [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. A lake half an inch off your course line is about 4 SM away on the ground, so do not expect it under the nose.

callout.text: Orient the chart to your heading and match shapes, not just names: the bend of a river, a highway crossing a railroad, a lake with a dam at one end. Two features that agree beat one that 'sort of' matches (application of [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]).

check.q: On a sectional, what does a small black circle with descriptive type mark?
check.a: A water, oil or gas tank [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p. 10]].

chunks.title: Fix your position with VOR and GPS

body.p: With a VOR or ADF receiver you can find your position by plotting an azimuth from two or more stations; where the lines cross is your fix [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Center the needle and the course selector shows the radial (with FROM) or its reciprocal course to the station (with TO) [[1:411|PHAK 16-24]]. Draw the FROM radial outward from the station's compass rose on the chart.

bullets: Identify each station by its Morse code or recorded voice ID. Do not rely on FSS voice on the frequency, because one FSS may talk over several VORs with other names [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]].
No ID means the station may be down for maintenance; do not use it [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]].

The NAV flag shows when the signal is too weak, because you are too far away or too low for line of sight [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]]. At 1,000 ft AGL reception is about 40 to 45 miles, and it grows with altitude [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]]. One more reason to climb.
Use radio navigation to back up pilotage, not replace it; that is your safeguard against disorientation if a radio fails [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].

body.p: GPS can show your position and the nearest airport [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. But many VFR receivers and all hand-held units have no RAIM alerting, so a bad position can appear with no warning [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]]. If there is no RAIM, be suspicious of the GPS any time it disagrees with radio navigation, pilotage or dead reckoning [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]. VFR pilots should never rely on one system [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]].

callout.text: An out-of-date database can show airspace and waypoints that have moved or no longer exist. Without a current database, disregard the moving map for critical navigation decisions [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]. A lost pilot who trusts a stale map can fly straight into the airspace he was trying to avoid.
Cross-check rule for the checkride: give the examiner two independent answers that agree, for example a two-VOR fix and a landmark, or GPS and a VOR radial plus a town name.

check.q: You center the needle on a VOR with 045 in the course selector and a FROM flag. What line do you draw on the chart?
check.a: The 045 radial, drawn outward from the station; a centered needle with FROM shows the radial you are on [[1:411|PHAK 16-24]].

chunks.title: Who can help, and how to reach them

body.p: ATC and flight service specialists are the best external resources in flight [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]]. Use the frequencies shown on the sectional to reach any facility you can [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Help comes in the form of radio, radar, direction finding stations and other aircraft [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

head: Help
What you need
Source
rows: You can talk to the facility, you are inside radar coverage, and you can be radar identified
A facility with DF; you key the mike a few seconds, release, and turn when asked
FSSs provide search and rescue services and help lost aircraft and aircraft in emergencies
Guarded by DF stations, some aircraft, most civil towers, military towers and radar facilities
Given on request or if distress is declared; may be started for urgency in unusual cases

body.p: Reading the chart boxes: a heavy-line box is a Flight Service Station, and frequencies transmit and receive except those followed by R, which means receive only [[2:51|Chart Users' Guide p. 51]]. A thin-line box is a Remote Communications Outlet: frequencies above it are remoted to that NAVAID site, and the controlling FSS name is shown with it [[2:51|Chart Users' Guide p. 51]]. Many FSSs also talk on the VOR frequency [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]], so with an 'R' frequency you transmit on it and listen on the VOR (application). For Class C, magenta boxes give the approach control frequency for arriving VFR aircraft [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p. 16]].

callout.text: Vectors are advisory. Flying safely and obeying the CFRs stays your job [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]]. A controller may not be able to give vectors because of radar limits, traffic or workload, and that decision is not subject to question [[33:218|AIM 4-1-17e]]. Have a plan B.
Remote radio sites at VORs may let you hear a station you cannot reach. Higher altitude increases VHF line-of-sight range [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].

check.q: What three conditions does the AIM list for a VFR aircraft to get radar vectors?
check.a: It can communicate with the facility, it is within radar coverage, and it can be radar identified [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

body.p: You can get help just by calling the facility, stating the problem, your intentions and the help you want. The ICAO words have real advantages, though [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. Start with MAYDAY, preferably three times, for distress, or PAN-PAN for urgency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. MAYDAY has absolute priority and silences the frequency; PAN-PAN has priority over everything except distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

head: Situation
Transponder
Source
rows: Already talking to ATC on an assigned or VFR code
Keep that code and Mode C unless told otherwise
Want to alert a radar facility to distress or urgency
Squawk 7700 with Mode C, then establish communications at once

body.p: Code 7700 normally sets off an alarm at every control position. You may be outside radar coverage, so keep squawking it and keep trying the radio [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].

Where to call: normally the facility you are already talking to. If you are not talking to anyone, call the facility whose area you are in. If nobody answers, broadcast to 'Any Station' [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. 121.5 MHz is limited to line of sight. Center emergency coverage usually does not reach as far as its radar, so if a Center does not answer on 121.5, call the nearest tower [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. Most facilities, even airliners, monitor 121.5 [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

After contact, comply with advice and instructions, ask when you do not understand, and do not change frequency unless you must. If you do, tell the station first; if you cannot talk on the new frequency, go straight back [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

callout.text: The PHAK says to use 121.5 and 7700 when the situation becomes threatening [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. The AIM gives the finer rule: keep your assigned code while you are in contact with ATC, and use 7700 when you cannot establish communications right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

check.q: You call Center on 121.5 and get no answer. What does the AIM suggest?
check.a: Call the nearest tower; Center emergency frequency coverage usually does not reach its radar limits [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

chunks.title: Fuel and daylight set the deadline

body.p: Lost is a navigation problem. Lost with little fuel or little daylight is a survival problem [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Know both numbers the moment you are unsure.

head: Rule or guidance
What it says
Source
rows: VFR fuel to begin a flight
Fuel to the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes by day or 45 minutes at night, at normal cruise
The same 30 minutes day and 45 minutes night
When to be on the ground
Before the flight time passes what you planned for your fuel, or the gauge shows low
Minutes until exhaustion, including reserve and gauge error allowance
Little or no delay acceptable; not an emergency; no priority
Declare an emergency due to low fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes

body.p: Conserve: power is fuel. Maximum endurance (the most time in the air) happens at the minimum power required, where fuel flow is lowest. Maximum range (the most distance) happens at a slightly higher speed, at L/D max [[1:266|PHAK 11-10]] [[1:265|PHAK 11-9]]. Holding while ATC works on your position calls for endurance; heading for a known airport calls for range. The real numbers are in your POH [[1:266|PHAK 11-10]].

In the sample table at 5,000 ft, pulling back from 2,600 to 2,200 rpm cuts fuel flow from 8.1 to 6.0 gallons per hour [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]. With 14 gallons left that is about 104 minutes versus 140 minutes.

Daylight: night begins at the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. An hour is lost when you fly east from one time zone into the next, and the PHAK warns it can matter even crossing one zone from west edge to east edge [[1:391|PHAK 16-4]]. Get the sunset time at the destination from FSS when you plan [[1:392|PHAK 16-5]]. A lost pilot at dusk loses the landmarks he is relying on (application).

callout.text: Fuel exhaustion and no-landing-site options are why the AFH says too many precautionary landings become forced landings: the pilot uses wishful thinking instead of reason [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

check.q: What should a pilot include when stating 'fuel remaining' to ATC?
check.a: The approximate minutes the flight can continue, including reserve fuel and an allowance for fuel gauge error [[34:349|P/CG Fuel Remaining]].

chunks.title: Distraction, task saturation and collision risk

body.p: A lost pilot is a busy pilot: chart, radios, GPS, passengers. A common accident factor is a distraction that pulls attention away from the instruments or the view outside [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. As workload rises, you work harder but get less done, then fix on one item. A task-saturated pilot loses awareness of other inputs and decides on incomplete information [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

Look at the pitfalls in Figure 2-15. Getting behind the aircraft can lead to loss of positional or situational awareness, where the pilot does not know the airplane's location or cannot see things getting worse [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. Get-there-itis and operating without adequate fuel reserves often ride along with it [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]].

bullets: Fix for overload: stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Aviate first, then navigate, then communicate (application).
Use the right seat: a passenger can watch for traffic or hold the chart [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]] [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Minimize head-down time with GPS and keep a sharp lookout for traffic, terrain and obstacles [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].
Near VFR waypoints, VORs and NDBs, other pilots converge on the same points. Use ATC services and turn on landing lights [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

callout.text: Disorientation is also a control problem. Many pilots not qualified for instrument flight cannot keep control when they meet clouds or reduced visibility [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. A lost VFR pilot pressing on under lowering clouds is two pitfalls at once: loss of positional awareness and VFR into IMC [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]].

check.q: According to the PHAK, what should a pilot do when a work overload situation exists?
check.a: Stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

chunks.title: When to ask, when to declare

body.p: Pilots declare emergencies for fire or engine failure without a second thought, but many are reluctant to report an urgency condition that is not yet perilous but could become catastrophic [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. The AIM is blunt: request assistance immediately; delay has caused accidents and cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

Time is a resource too. ATC may be very useful if you are lost, but in a real emergency there may be no time to contact ATC [[30:56|RMH 8-3]] [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]]. That is the case for calling early, while you still have fuel, daylight and altitude to work with.

head: Stage
Typical clues
Action
Source
rows: Missed checkpoint, GPS and VOR disagree
Hold heading, climb, try to fix position; you are already in urgency
Still unsure after a few minutes, fuel or daylight getting short
Call ATC or FSS; PAN-PAN; ask for vectors or DF
Fuel nearly gone, or VFR flight ahead no longer possible
MAYDAY; 7700 if no contact; plan a landing

body.p: Declaring an emergency brings extra help and priority handling [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. If VFR is no longer possible ahead and you are not instrument rated, tell the controller you are not instrument rated and declare distress [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. If a VFR route to a safe landing exists, choose it over a vector into IFR weather [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

callout.text: Emergency authority: in an emergency needing immediate action you may deviate from Part 91 to the extent needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. If you deviate from an ATC clearance, tell ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]].
'Confess' in the memory aid is AIM 6-1-2 in plain words: admit it early, when it is still urgency, not distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

check.q: You are not instrument rated, you are lost, and VFR flight ahead is no longer possible. What does the AIM say to tell the controller?
check.a: That you are not instrument rated, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

chunks.title: Choose the way out: continue, divert or land

body.p: Once you know where you are, decide where to go. Pick the option with the most margin, not the one closest to the original plan. Get-there-itis is a fixation on the original destination with a disregard for any other course of action [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. If the situation is an emergency, turn toward the new airport promptly rather than finishing every calculation first [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

bullets: Continue: only if your position is confirmed by two sources and fuel and daylight still give a real reserve (application).
Divert: the nearest suitable airport; GPS can show the nearest one [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. If you are on a flight plan and land somewhere else, report it to FSS [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

Precautionary landing: being lost, a fuel shortage and worsening weather are listed reasons. It is less hazardous than a forced landing because you choose the field and can use power [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

body.p: If you must land off an airport: activate the ELT if the installation allows, and after a crash landing, stay with the airplane unless you have good reason to think you will not be found [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]]. Since 2009 satellites no longer listen for 121.5 MHz ELTs, so an older ELT depends on a nearby ATC facility or an overflying aircraft hearing it [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. A 406 MHz personal locator beacon is encouraged for pilots who do not own the airplane [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
Ground signals tell searchers what you need. V means require assistance, X means require medical assistance, and symbols should be at least 10 feet high with strong contrast [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

callout.text: The AFH lists 'reluctance to accept the emergency situation' as a psychological hazard: indecision and delay while trying to fix what went wrong at the expense of control [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. Make the landing decision while you still have power and choices.

check.q: Why is a precautionary landing usually less hazardous than a forced landing?
check.a: You have more time to pick the terrain and plan the approach, and you can use power to correct errors [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

head: Error
Fix
Source
rows: Turning toward every feature that might be the checkpoint
Hold the heading and look for the next checkpoint
No times on the log, so no last known position
Write the time at every checkpoint; it goes in the emergency call
Staying low to 'see better' and losing radio, radar and VOR reception
Climb, staying VFR and clear of terrain
Trusting a GPS with no RAIM over a landmark that disagrees
Cross-check with VOR, pilotage and dead reckoning
Waiting to call until fuel is low
Call when doubtful; that is already urgency
Squawking 7700 while already working ATC on an assigned code
Keep the assigned code unless told otherwise
Changing frequency in the middle of getting help
Tell the station first, or return if contact fails
Giving fuel in gallons or 'about an hour'
Give minutes, including reserve and gauge error
Pressing on toward the original destination at dusk
Divert or make a precautionary landing while you still have options

callout.text: On the checkride, talk through every step: 'Holding heading 270, climbing to 4,500 below the clouds, last fix the dam at 1412, tuning the VOR to the south.' The examiner grades the method as much as the answer.

check.q: What is the fix for giving ATC your fuel in gallons?
check.a: State fuel remaining as minutes of flight, including reserve and an allowance for gauge error [[34:349|P/CG Fuel Remaining]].

For 2,500, 5,000, 7,500 and 10,000 ft it lists rpm, percent power, true airspeed in mph, gallons per hour, and endurance and range for 38 and 48 gallons with no reserve. At 5,000 ft: 2,700 rpm burns 9.0 gph, 2,600 rpm 8.1 gph, 2,500 rpm 7.4 gph, 2,400 rpm 6.9 gph, 2,300 rpm 6.5 gph and 2,200 rpm 6.0 gph. The 2,400 rpm row is highlighted: 116 mph, 6.9 gph, 5.5 hours, 635 miles.

f3.caption: FAA Chart Users' Guide: Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF), with the man-made obstacle example. (Chart Users' Guide p. 12)
f3.alt: Text explaining the MEF and how it is computed for a man-made obstacle. Worked example: obstacle top 2,649 ft MSL, plus 100 ft possible error, equals 2,749, raised to 2,800, shown as a large blue 2 with a small 8. A sectional excerpt near Asheboro shows the 2,649 ft obstacle circled in yellow and the blue MEF figure 28 in the quadrant.

f4.caption: FAA Chart Users' Guide: obstruction symbols, an ATC checkpoint landmark and the group obstacle symbol. (Chart Users' Guide p. 11)
f4.alt: Symbols for obstacles under 1,000 ft AGL, 1,000 ft AGL or more, and wind turbines. A tall black smokestack symbol labeled Garfield Stack with 5540 MSL and 650 AGL in blue shows a man-made feature ATC uses as a checkpoint. A group obstacle symbol shows 4977 and 1432. A last example shows 5000 and 1500 UC for an obstacle under construction.

f5.caption: FAA Chart Users' Guide: Flight Service Station (FSS) and Remote Communications Outlet (RCO) boxes. (Chart Users' Guide p. 51)
f5.alt: Left: a heavy-line box Denver DEN; a Northway box with 122.1R above left, 123.6 above right, and 116.3 Ch 110 ORT inside; an Iliamna box with 123.6 above. Text says heavy line boxes are FSSs and R means receive only. Right: a thin-line Olympia RCO box with 123.6 above and McChord underlined below; a Frederick box with 122.1R above, 109.9 FDK inside and Leesburg below; a Togiak box with 122.25 above and Kenai below.

f6.caption: Figure 2-15. Typical operational pitfalls requiring pilot awareness. (PHAK 2-22)
f6.alt: A table of twelve operational pitfalls with short definitions: peer pressure, mindset, get-there-itis, duck-under syndrome, scud running, continuing VFR into instrument conditions, getting behind the aircraft, loss of positional or situational awareness, operating without adequate fuel reserves, descent below the minimum en route altitude, flying outside the envelope, and neglect of flight planning, preflight inspections and checklists.

f7.caption: FIG 6-2-1. Ground-Air Visual Code for Use by Survivors. (AIM 6-2-8)
f7.alt: A table of ground symbols: V means require assistance, X require medical assistance, N no, Y yes, and an arrow proceeding in this direction. If in doubt, use SOS. Instructions: make symbols at least 10 feet high from any material with strong color contrast; on snow, tramp or dig them; the pilot acknowledges by rocking the wings.

scenario.title: The photo flight that circled itself lost
scenario.setup: You are a new commercial pilot flying an aerial photo job in a four-seat high-wing single with a photographer aboard. For 25 minutes you have circled farms and shot photos at 2,000 ft AGL in rolling country, using a tablet GPS. Your log shows your last confirmed fix over a reservoir dam at 1340, and since then you have flown about 110 knots between orbits. It is now 1405. The tablet battery dies. The farms all look alike and the ceiling is about 4,500 ft MSL. You have 20 gallons on board, burning 9 gallons per hour. Sunset is at 1455.

questions.q: What do you do in the first minute?
questions.a: Stop circling, roll out and hold a heading [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Then climb as far as the clouds allow, staying VFR, to improve radio, navigation and radar range [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]] [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]]. You are already in an urgency condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

questions.q: How big is your 'where could I be' circle, and why is the answer misleading?
questions.a: 25 minutes at 110 knots is 25 x 110 / 60 = 45.8, so up to about 46 NM from the dam (dead reckoning [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]). Because most of that time was spent in orbits, you are probably much closer; but with no recorded headings you cannot narrow it, which is why times and headings matter [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: Your panel VOR shows a NAV flag on the station you tune. What could be the reason, and what helps?
questions.a: You may be too far away or too low for line of sight, or the station may be out of service; check the ID [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]]. Climbing increases VOR reception range [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].

questions.q: How much fuel and daylight do you have, and which one limits you?
questions.a: 20 / 9 x 60 = 133 minutes of fuel, but sunset is in 50 minutes [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Daylight is the tighter limit for finding landmarks, and night itself begins only at the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

questions.q: You reach approach control. What do you tell them?
questions.a: Your call sign and type, that you are unsure of position, weather, intentions and request, last known position (the dam at 1340) and heading since, altitude, fuel remaining in minutes and people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]] [[34:349|P/CG Fuel Remaining]]. Use PAN-PAN if you want urgency handling [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

questions.q: The photographer asks you to 'just finish the last two farms' once you are found. How do you decide?
questions.a: That is get-there-itis and peer pressure, two listed pitfalls [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. With sunset close and fuel used up in orbits, the commercial answer is to take the vectors to the nearest suitable airport and land; continuing is wishful thinking [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

skills.do: Use an appropriate method to find your position: landmarks, dead reckoning from the last fix, a two-station VOR fix, or GPS cross-checked against another source. No numeric tolerance is given.
skills.practice: On dual cross-countries, have your CFI cover the GPS and ask 'where are we?' Answer with two methods that agree [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]] [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]].

skills.do: Keep an appropriate heading and climb as needed, staying VFR and watching for traffic.
skills.practice: When a checkpoint does not appear, call out 'holding heading' and plan a VFR climb before touching the chart [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]] [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

skills.do: Identify prominent landmarks and match them to the chart.
skills.practice: On every flight, name one large feature and one confirming feature for each checkpoint, using chart symbols for tanks, landmarks and obstacles [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p. 10]] [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p. 11]].

skills.do: Use navigation systems or facilities, or contact an ATC facility for help, with correct phraseology and transponder use.
skills.practice: Practice the urgency call out loud with last known position, time and fuel in minutes; find the FSS, RCO and approach frequencies on the chart before each flight [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]] [[2:51|Chart Users' Guide p. 51]].

skills.do: Select an appropriate course of action: continue, divert, ask for help, declare an emergency or make a precautionary landing.
skills.practice: On each cross-country, brief a 'lost plan': nearest airports along the route, fuel and daylight limits, and the point where you will land instead of searching [[24:350|AFH 18-1]] [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

activities.title: True or false: the first minute
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: If you miss a checkpoint, turn toward the feature you think it might be.
cards.why: False. Hold the heading and look for the next checkpoint; turning away from the heading makes it easy to become lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

cards.s: Climbing increases radio and navigation reception range and radar coverage.
Radar and ADS-B surveillance coverage is line of sight, so a low airplane can lose contact.
cards.why: True. Low altitude or antenna shielding can reduce range; climbing can improve coverage [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]].

cards.s: An MEF is rounded down to the nearest 100 ft so it is never too high.
cards.why: False. MEFs are rounded up to the next 100 ft value [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p. 12]].

cards.s: When lost in IFR conditions in controlled airspace, the AIM lets you climb whenever you want.
cards.why: False. Unauthorized climb or descent under IFR conditions in controlled airspace is prohibited, except under 14 CFR 91.3(b) [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]].

cards.s: The PHAK tells a lost pilot to read a town's name on its water tower if possible.

activities.title: Build a two-VOR fix
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Tune the first VOR from the chart and positively identify its Morse code
Check that no NAV flag shows
Turn the course selector until the needle centers with a FROM indication
Draw that radial outward from the station's compass rose on the chart
Repeat with a second station and draw its radial
Your position is where the two lines cross; confirm it with a landmark

activities.title: Who answers on which frequency?
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Frequency the FSS only receives on
Frequency remoted to an RCO site

activities.title: Squawk 7700 or keep your code?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then tap what the AIM says to set.

items.t: On flight following with code 3317 when you realize you are unsure of position
Lost, not talking to anyone, and no answer yet on any frequency you tried
Getting radar vectors from approach on code 0452
The controller you are working tells you to squawk 7700
Low on fuel and lost, radio calls unanswered, wanting to alert any radar facility
Declared an emergency with Center while on an assigned discrete code, no new instruction

activities.title: Lost-pilot numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Figure 11-27, 5,000 ft, 2,600 rpm: 8.1 gal/hr. You have 14 gallons left. About how many minutes of fuel remain?
items.why: 14 / 8.1 = 1.728 hr; x 60 = 103.7, about 104 minutes [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]. Report it as minutes, including reserve and gauge error [[34:349|P/CG Fuel Remaining]].

items.q: Same airplane and altitude, you pull back to 2,200 rpm: 6.0 gal/hr. How many minutes do the same 14 gallons last?
items.why: 14 / 6.0 = 2.333 hr; x 60 = 140 minutes, about 36 minutes more than at 2,600 rpm [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]. Lower power moves you toward maximum endurance [[1:266|PHAK 11-10]].

items.q: Last confirmed fix at 1412. It is 1430 and your groundspeed has been about 110 knots. What is the farthest you could be from that fix?
items.why: 18 minutes x 110 knots / 60 = 33 NM, from time and groundspeed (dead reckoning [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]).

items.q: The highest feature in a quadrant is a natural hilltop at 3,212 ft MSL. Using the Chart Users' Guide method (add 100 ft vertical error and a 200 ft obstacle allowance, then round up to the next 100 ft), what MEF is charted, in feet?
items.why: 3,212 + 100 + 200 = 3,512, raised to the next 100 ft = 3,600 ft, shown as a large 3 and small 6 [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p. 13]] [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p. 12]].

items.q: Your VFR flight plan ETA is 1530 local and you have not reached anyone. At what time (hhmm) does the AIM say a search will start if you do not respond?
items.why: If you fail to respond within one-half hour after your ETA, a search will be started: 1530 + 30 minutes = 1600 [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

activities.title: Name the pitfall
activities.intro: Tap a lost pilot's thought, then the Figure 2-15 pitfall it shows.

pairs.l: "The passengers paid for this destination, we are pressing on."
"I have no idea which town that is, and I did not notice the weather closing in."
pairs.r: Loss of positional or situational awareness

pairs.l: "We left with exactly enough fuel; the reserve is just extra."
"I'll stay low under this cloud deck, in the mist, so I can keep seeing the roads."
"I know this route; I didn't bother with the chart or a nav log."
pairs.r: Neglect of flight planning, preflight inspections, and checklists

activities.title: Lost at dusk with passengers
activities.intro: You are flying a commercial sightseeing flight in a four-seat single, VFR at 3,500 ft, with two passengers. Planned fuel at landing was 45 minutes. Sunset is in 35 minutes. You realize the lake below is not the one on your course line.

options: Turn toward the nearest lake on the chart that looks similar
Hold your heading and note the time
Descend to 1,500 ft AGL to read road signs
Call the passengers' attention to the lake as a 'scenic detour'
steps.why: If confused, hold the heading; turning away is how pilots become lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. The time starts your last-known-position record [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

steps.s: Clouds are well above you. You climb to 5,500 ft. The VOR to the east now shows no flag and identifies correctly. What next?
options: Fly to that VOR and wait over it
Get a second VOR radial and cross it with the first, then confirm with a landmark
Trust the first radial alone and fly it outbound
Switch the transponder to 7700 and wait for a call
steps.why: Plot azimuths from two or more stations for a fix [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]], identify each station [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]], and cross-check with pilotage [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]].

steps.s: The fix still does not make sense and 10 minutes have passed. What do you do?
options: Keep trying alone; calling ATC would look unprofessional
Call approach on the chart frequency, say you are unsure of position, and ask for help
Turn back toward where you think you came from
Descend to look for the original course line
steps.why: You were in an urgency condition the moment you became doubtful; this is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Use the frequencies on the chart and accept radar vectors [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

steps.s: Approach is too busy to vector you. You have 50 minutes of fuel and 25 minutes of daylight. What now?
options: Wait on frequency until the controller has time
Declare an emergency (PAN-PAN or MAYDAY as fits) to get priority, or call FSS or 121.5
Turn off the radio to concentrate on the chart
Climb into the clouds to get better radar coverage
steps.why: Controllers may decline vectors for workload [[33:218|AIM 4-1-17e]]. Declaring an emergency brings additional help and priority handling [[30:47|RMH 6-4]], and 121.5 is guarded by radar facilities and towers [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. Climbing into cloud violates VFR minimums [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]].

steps.s: ATC finds you 22 miles south of course. The nearest lighted airport is 9 miles away; your destination is 30 miles. What do you choose?
options: The destination, because the passengers expect it
The nearby airport, and tell ATC and FSS of the change
Hold over the nearby airport until the passengers agree
The destination at maximum range speed
steps.why: With little daylight and a reduced reserve, choose margin over the original goal; get-there-itis is a listed pitfall [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. Report the landing to FSS if on a flight plan [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

quiz.q: How do the private and commercial ACS Tasks for lost procedures compare?
options: The commercial Task adds a heading tolerance of 10 degrees
The elements are the same; neither gives a number tolerance
The commercial Task drops the risk elements
The private Task requires declaring an emergency; the commercial does not
quiz.why: Both list K1 to K2, R1 to R4 and S1 to S5 with identical wording and no number tolerance (ACS CA.VI.D; ACS PA.VI.D).

quiz.q: In the AIM emergency message, what position do you give if you are lost?
options: Your best guess of present position
Last known position, the time there, and the heading since
The nearest VOR and DME
Only your altitude and fuel
quiz.why: The AIM element is present position and heading, or if lost, last known position, time and heading since that position [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

quiz.q: What area does one MEF on a sectional cover?
options: A circle 10 NM around each airport
A quadrant bounded by ticked lines every 30 minutes of latitude and 30 minutes of longitude
One degree of latitude by one degree of longitude
The area between two VOR radials
quiz.why: A quadrant on sectionals is bounded by ticked lines dividing each 30 minutes of latitude and each 30 minutes of longitude [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p. 12]].

quiz.q: A town you want as a checkpoint is 0.75 inch from your course line on a sectional. About how far is it from your course, in nautical miles?
options: About 3.4 NM
About 5.1 NM
About 6.0 NM
About 8.0 NM

quiz.q: Why should you not use FSS voice on a VOR frequency to identify the station?
options: FSS voice is only broadcast at night
One FSS may transmit over several VORs with different names
FSS voice is always out of date
VORs do not carry voice
quiz.why: Many FSSs remotely transmit over several omniranges with names different from the FSS, so identify by Morse code or the VOR's recorded voice ID [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]].

quiz.q: ATC is giving you radar vectors as a lost VFR pilot. Who is responsible for flying the aircraft safely and obeying the CFRs?
options: The controller, while vectors are being given
You, the pilot; the vectors are advisory
The controller for terrain, you for traffic
Nobody until you are found
quiz.why: Radar navigational assistance is advisory, does not authorize you to violate the CFRs, and flying the aircraft safely remains with the pilot [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

quiz.q: You want to reach approach control before entering a Class C area near you. Where on the sectional is its VFR arrival frequency shown?
options: In the airport data block under the runway length
In a magenta box note near the Class C
Only in the Chart Supplement
In the FSS heavy-line box
quiz.why: Separate notes in magenta boxes give the approach control frequencies for arriving VFR aircraft to call before entering Class C [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p. 16]].

quiz.q: Which priority does a PAN-PAN call have?
options: Over all communications, including distress
Over all communications except distress
Equal to routine traffic
Only on 121.5
quiz.why: Urgency communications have priority over all other communications except distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

quiz.q: Where is maximum endurance found on the power-required curve?
options: At L/D max
At minimum power required, where fuel flow is lowest
At maximum cruise power
At the stall speed
quiz.why: Maximum endurance is at minimum power required; maximum range is at L/D max [[1:266|PHAK 11-10]] [[1:265|PHAK 11-9]].

quiz.q: What does the AIM say to do after a crash landing, in most cases?
options: Walk to the nearest road at once
Stay with the aircraft and prepare to signal searchers
Burn the aircraft to make smoke
Fly the ELT antenna to high ground
quiz.why: Unless you have good reason to think you will not be found, it is best to remain with the aircraft and prepare means of signaling [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

final_quiz.q: Twelve minutes after missing a checkpoint, you are still unsure of position but have plenty of fuel and good weather. A friend says you are not in an emergency yet. Per the AIM, what is your status?
options: Normal; urgency starts only at low fuel
At least an urgency condition, and the time to ask for help
Distress, requiring MAYDAY
Minimum fuel
final_quiz.why: An aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Distress means serious or imminent danger [[34:337|P/CG Distress]].

final_quiz.q: Lost at 1,200 ft AGL under a 4,000 ft MSL overcast with the field area near 1,000 ft MSL, you get NAV flags on both VORs and no answer from approach. What is the best single change?
options: Descend to read signs
Climb as high as VFR cloud clearance allows
Turn 180 degrees and hold altitude
Turn the transponder off
final_quiz.why: Altitude improves radio and navigation reception and radar coverage [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]; VOR range grows with altitude [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]]. In Class E below 10,000 ft you must stay 500 ft below clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]].

final_quiz.q: Your hand-held GPS (no RAIM) puts you 7 NM east of where a two-VOR fix and a stadium symbol on the chart agree. What should you believe?
options: The GPS, because satellites are more accurate
The VOR fix and the landmark, and treat the GPS as suspect
Average the two positions
Neither; call 121.5 before doing anything
final_quiz.why: Without RAIM, be suspicious of the GPS when it disagrees with other navigation, pilotage or dead reckoning [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]; two independent sources agree here [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p. 10]].

final_quiz.q: Lost and talking to no one, you squawk 7700. Several minutes pass with no radio contact. What does the AIM say?
options: Return to 1200, since 7700 has failed
Keep squawking 7700 and keep trying to establish communications; you may be outside radar coverage
Switch to 7600
Turn the transponder off to save power
final_quiz.why: You might not be within radar coverage, so continue squawking 7700 and establish radio communications as soon as possible [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].

final_quiz.q: You call Center on 121.5 MHz in a remote area and get no reply, though you are in Center radar coverage. What explains it, and what next?
options: Center never monitors 121.5; give up on it
Center emergency frequency coverage usually does not reach its radar limits; call the nearest tower
121.5 is only for ELTs
Switch to 243.0 and wait
final_quiz.why: Normally ARTCC emergency frequency capability does not extend to radar coverage limits; if Center does not answer on 121.5, call the nearest tower [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

final_quiz.q: You hear a station on its RCO frequency clearly but it never answers you. What is the most likely reason?
options: Your transponder is off
Remote sites may transmit to you but not receive you; climb or try another frequency
RCOs work only at night
You must use DF first
final_quiz.why: At remote sites you can sometimes hear but not reach the ground station's receiver; higher altitude increases VHF range [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].

final_quiz.q: Lost with 11 gallons left at 8.1 gal/hr, you call approach. What fuel figure fits the AIM?
options: 'Eleven gallons'
'About 80 minutes,' a figure that includes reserve and gauge error allowance
'Minimum fuel,' which gives you priority
'Enough for an hour plus reserve'
final_quiz.why: 11 / 8.1 x 60 = 81.5, about 80 minutes. Fuel remaining is stated in minutes including reserve and gauge error [[34:349|P/CG Fuel Remaining]]. Minimum fuel does not imply priority [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].

final_quiz.q: ATC is vectoring you, a non-instrument-rated pilot, and the vector heads toward lowering clouds while clear weather lies to the west. What does the AIM advise?
options: Follow the vector; ATC is responsible for terrain
Tell ATC the weather and choose the VFR option to the west
Climb through the clouds on the vector
Stop talking and turn west without telling ATC
final_quiz.why: Keep the controller advised of weather; non-instrument pilots should choose a VFR course over a vector into IFR conditions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Vectors are advisory [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

final_quiz.q: You land at a different airport than your VFR flight plan destination after getting lost. What does the AIM require of you?
options: Nothing; the plan closes automatically
Report the landing to the nearest FSS and give your original destination
Call the destination tower only
Wait one hour, then call
final_quiz.why: If you land somewhere other than the intended destination, report to the nearest FSS with your original destination; flight plans are not closed automatically [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

final_quiz.q: Which pair is correct for a lost pilot trying to stretch fuel while waiting for help, versus trying to reach a known airport?
options: Endurance at L/D max; range at minimum power
Endurance at minimum power required; range at L/D max
Both at maximum cruise power
Both at stall speed plus 5 knots
final_quiz.why: Maximum endurance is at minimum power required; maximum range is at L/D max [[1:266|PHAK 11-10]].

final_quiz.q: You are lost at night. A controller asks you to hold the mike button for a few seconds, release it, then turn 90 degrees and repeat. What service is this?
options: Radar identification by squawk
Direction finding (DF) assistance
Minimum safe altitude warning
Intercept and escort
final_quiz.why: In DF assistance the controller asks you to key the mike for a few seconds and may ask for turns, then plots your position [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

final_quiz.q: Flying an eastbound charter in the late afternoon, you get lost near a time zone boundary. Why does the PHAK warn about this kind of flight even before you get lost?
options: Eastbound flights burn more fuel
An hour is lost going east, so darkness can arrive earlier than expected
VORs are not usable across time zones
Flight plans expire at the boundary
final_quiz.why: Time zones must be considered on eastward flights that must finish before dark; an hour is lost going east [[1:391|PHAK 16-4]].

final_quiz.q: After a forced landing in a remote field with an injured passenger, which ground symbol asks for medical help?
options: V
X
N
Y
final_quiz.why: X means require medical assistance; V means require assistance [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

takeaways: Doubtful about position equals urgency. Ask for help then, not later.
First minute: hold the heading, note the time, climb if VFR and traffic allow.
Fix position two ways that agree: landmarks, two VOR radials, GPS with a cross-check.
Help is on the chart: approach, FSS and RCO boxes, 121.5. Keep the assigned code if in contact; 7700 if not.
Fuel in minutes and minutes of daylight are the deadline. Pull power back toward endurance while you sort it out.
Declare early for priority; vectors are advisory and may be refused.
If the margin is gone, divert or make a precautionary landing while you still have choices.
cfi_notes: The commercial ACS text for this Task is identical to the private one, so raise the bar in the oral: expect fuel in minutes, a written last known position, and a clear divert or land decision, not just 'I would call ATC.'

The 'Cs' memory aid (climb, communicate, confess, comply, conserve, circle) is not in the FAA sources used here. Climb, communicate and comply are in PHAK 16-34 and AIM 6-3-2; 'confess' matches AIM 6-1-2; 'conserve' fits PHAK 11-10 endurance. 'Circle' conflicts with the PHAK 'if confused, hold the heading' line, so teach it only as orbiting over an identified landmark.

PHAK 16-34 says to use 121.5 and 7700 when the situation becomes threatening. The AIM 6-3-2 rule is more precise: keep the assigned code while in contact with ATC and squawk 7700 when unable to establish communications. Teach the AIM.

PHAK 2-24 lists En Route Flight Advisory Service (Flight Watch) among FSS services. The current AIM 4-1-3 list of FSS services does not include it; teach the AIM list and do not send students looking for Flight Watch.
Students often confuse 'minimum fuel' with an emergency. AIM 5-5-15 says it is not an emergency and gives no priority; if priority is needed, declare an emergency for low fuel and give minutes.

Use the photo-flight or sightseeing scenario: commercial work often involves orbits and low altitude, which destroy dead reckoning. Have the student fly orbits, then cover the GPS and ask for a last known position and time.

Make the student find the approach, FSS/RCO and 121.5 options on the sectional before each cross-country and say them out loud. Under stress, finding a frequency is where heads-down time and collisions happen.
AIM 6-2-4 notes satellites stopped monitoring 121.5 MHz ELTs in 2009. Ask students what kind of ELT the airplane has; it changes how quickly anyone will come looking.
gaps: The ACS Skills elements for this Task give no numeric tolerances; the examiner judges the method and the choice.
No FAA source used here gives a lost-procedure checklist or the 'Cs' list; the sequence is built from PHAK 16-34, PHAK 16-12 and AIM 6-1-2, 6-3-1 and 6-3-2.
Maximum endurance and maximum range speeds and power settings are airplane-specific and come from the POH/AFM; Figure 11-27 is only a sample.
The sources do not say which facilities still offer DF steering or where radar coverage ends at low altitude; ask ATC or check current FAA publications.
Sunset and civil twilight times are not given in these sources; the PHAK says to get sunset from FSS and the AFH mentions an FAA online tool.
No source here says how long to search before calling or landing; that personal minimum belongs in a CFI-guided risk assessment.
